Interpretation of Local and Kaggle Results

The distinction between local validation and Kaggle evaluation is especially important for this classification problem.

Local validation evaluates predictions against known labels in a held-out portion of the training data. It therefore permits the calculation of accuracy, F1, and related metrics.

Kaggle evaluates submitted predictions against hidden competition labels.

The two evaluations can differ because:
  
  •	  the observations are different;
  •	  the competition test distribution may differ from the validation distribution;
  •	  the validation design may not perfectly reproduce the competition evaluation;
  •	  class frequencies may differ;
  •	  geographic and temporal patterns may change across the datasets.

Consequently, the Kaggle scores should be reported as external competition results rather than interpreted as direct replacements for the local validation metrics.

## Crime Classification Findings

Several findings are supported by the analysis.

First, all three required models extracted useful information from the available predictors because their validation accuracies exceeded the baseline accuracy of 0.1992.

Second, the Random Forest increased validation accuracy relative to the Decision Tree and produced substantially lower log loss.

Third, the SVM produced accuracy nearly identical to the Random Forest while achieving higher reported macro and weighted F1 values.

Fourth, the Decision Tree produced the highest reported macro F1 among the three models.

These results demonstrate that model performance depends on the metric used for evaluation.

The analysis therefore does not treat a single metric as a complete representation of classification quality. 

Instead, the results are interpreted using accuracy, macro F1, weighted F1, log loss, and the confusion matrix.

The classification analysis also demonstrates the importance of feature construction and leakage control. 
Excluding variables that directly encode the outcome helps ensure that the models are evaluated using predictors that are more appropriate for the intended prediction task.

# Cross-Analysis Findings

The three analytical components of Assignment 8 demonstrate how model development depends on the structure of the prediction problem, the characteristics of the available data, and the evaluation criterion used to assess performance.

The Store Sales analysis addressed a forecasting problem in which observations are ordered in time. The House Prices analysis addressed a continuous-response regression problem involving numerous numerical and categorical predictors. The San Francisco Crime analysis addressed a high-dimensional multiclass classification problem.

Although the modeling techniques differed substantially, several common findings emerged.
Model Complexity Does Not Guarantee Better Predictive Performance

One of the most consistent findings across the three analyses is that a more complex model does not automatically produce better validation performance.

For Store Sales, the 7-day moving-average benchmark achieved a validation RMSE of approximately 109,822. This was slightly lower than the RMSE values for both required forecasting models:
  
  •	  ETS RMSE = 113,065.78
  •	  ARIMA(1,1,1) RMSE = 111,986.09

This demonstrates that a relatively simple forecasting method can perform competitively when recent observations contain substantial information about the near-term future.

***The House Prices analysis produced a similar finding***. 

PCA reduced the encoded predictor space from 290 variables to 71 components while retaining approximately 95.07% of the variance. Nevertheless, the PCA Ridge model had a higher validation Log RMSE than the engineered linear regression:

  •	  Engineered Linear Regression Log RMSE = 0.1704
  •	  PCA Ridge Regression Log RMSE = 0.1962

The dimensionality reduction therefore achieved a substantial reduction in predictor dimensionality without producing better validation performance under the selected metric.

These findings reinforce the principle that model selection should be based on empirical validation rather than the assumption that a more sophisticated algorithm will necessarily generalize better.

***Feature Engineering Can Improve Model Representation***

The House Prices analysis demonstrated the value of feature engineering.

The regression analysis included:
  
  •	  polynomial terms;
  •	  interaction terms;
  •	  age-related variables;
  •	  categorical encoding;
  •	  response transformation;
  •	  subset selection; and
  •	PCA-based dimension reduction.

The polynomial terms allow the model to represent curvature. For example, the effect of living area on price may not remain constant across the entire range of property sizes.

The interaction terms allow the effect of one predictor to depend on another predictor. For example, the association between living area and price can differ according to overall property quality.

The age variables provide additional information about the relationship between property age, remodeling, and sale price.

These transformations demonstrate that predictive performance depends not only on the statistical algorithm but also on how the underlying data-generating structure is represented.

## Validation Must Match the Prediction Problem

The three analyses also demonstrate why validation procedures should reflect the structure of the prediction task.

For Store Sales, a chronological validation split was used because future observations should not be used to predict earlier observations.

For House Prices, a separate validation sample was used to evaluate competing regression specifications.

For Crime Classification, a held-out validation sample was used to evaluate classification accuracy and class-level performance.

The appropriate validation design therefore depends on the prediction problem.

Randomly mixing observations in a time-series problem can create temporal information leakage, while an ordinary random split in a geographically and temporally clustered classification problem may not fully reproduce the conditions of future prediction.

Consequently, validation results should always be interpreted in the context of how the validation sample was constructed.

## Different Metrics Answer Different Questions

A major cross-analysis finding is that no single metric provides a complete description of model performance.

For Store Sales, MAE and RMSE produced slightly different comparisons between ETS and ARIMA.

For House Prices, raw-scale and log-scale evaluation produced substantially different interpretations. Model A had a raw-scale RMSE of 63,125 but a log-scale RMSE of 0.1704.

For Crime Classification, accuracy, macro F1, weighted F1, and log loss produced different model comparisons.

This occurs because the metrics emphasize different aspects of prediction.

MAE treats absolute errors linearly, while RMSE gives greater weight to large errors.

Log-transformed regression metrics emphasize proportional differences more strongly than raw-dollar metrics.

Macro F1 gives each classification category equal weight, while weighted F1 incorporates class frequency.

Log loss evaluates the quality of predicted probabilities rather than only whether the most likely class was correct.

The interpretation of model performance must therefore begin with the question being answered by the metric.

## Assumptions Across the Three Analytical Problems

The assignment required investigation of assumptions associated with the selected models. The analysis approached this requirement differently for each problem because forecasting, regression, and classification models have different assumptions.

**Time-Series Assumptions**

The Store Sales analysis assumed that the aggregate daily series contained meaningful temporal structure that could be represented through trend and weekly seasonality.

The observed day-of-week pattern provided empirical evidence supporting a seven-day seasonal structure.
The ETS model therefore used a seasonal period of seven, while the ARIMA analysis considered several autoregressive and moving-average specifications.

**The analysis also investigated residual behavior**.

A well-specified forecasting model should leave residuals that do not contain substantial systematic temporal structure. If residuals retain strong autocorrelation, the model has not captured all predictable information in the series.

The saved residual artifacts provide evidence for evaluating this issue.

The analysis did not report numerical Ljung-Box statistics because those statistics were not included in the generated result artifacts. Reporting a numerical test that was not actually calculated would incorrectly imply additional analysis.

This distinction is important for reproducibility.

**Regression Assumptions**

The House Prices analysis considered the major assumptions relevant to linear regression:

  •	  linearity;
  •	  constant variance;
  •	  independence;
  •	  residual behavior;
  •	  influential observations; and
  •	  multicollinearity.

The use of polynomial and interaction terms was specifically intended to allow more flexible relationships than a simple linear specification.

The log transformation of SalePrice also addressed the strong positive skew commonly associated with monetary outcomes and reduced the influence of extremely expensive observations on the transformed response scale.

The high-dimensional encoded predictor matrix created potential multicollinearity concerns. The PCA Ridge model provided an alternative approach in which correlated predictors were transformed into orthogonal principal components before regression.

The residual diagnostic artifacts should be interpreted as evidence about the extent to which the fitted model conforms to these assumptions.

No diagnostic should be interpreted as proving that an assumption is perfectly satisfied. Statistical assumptions are modeling approximations, and the objective is to determine whether violations are substantial enough to affect the intended analysis.

**Classification Assumptions**

Classification models have different requirements from ordinary linear regression.

The Crime Classification analysis focused on:

  •	  class imbalance;
  •	  independence;
  •	  feature representation;
  •	  potential leakage;
  •	  tree complexity; and
  •	  the adequacy of the SVM representation.
  
Class imbalance was particularly important because overall accuracy can be strongly influenced by common classes.

The relatively low macro F1 values demonstrate that classification performance varies across crime categories.

The exclusion of Descript and Resolution from the primary feature set also addressed potential leakage concerns.

The analysis therefore considered not only whether the models could predict the response, but also whether the predictors represented information that was appropriate for the intended prediction task.

## Comparative Discussion of the Three Problems

The three competitions required fundamentally different forms of statistical reasoning.

**Forecasting**

The Store Sales problem emphasized temporal dependence.

The most important structural findings were:

  •	  strong weekly seasonality;
  •	  substantial holiday effects;
  •	  changing sales levels over time; and
  •	  the importance of recent observations for short-horizon prediction.

The forecasting models therefore needed to account for temporal structure rather than treating observations as independent.

**Regression**

The House Prices problem emphasized the relationship between a continuous response and a large collection of predictors.

The analysis demonstrated that:

  •	  categorical variables require appropriate encoding;
  •	  nonlinear relationships can be represented with polynomial terms;
  •	  interactions allow conditional relationships;
  •	  response transformations can substantially affect model behavior;
  •	  correlated predictors motivate dimension-reduction or regularization approaches.

The regression analysis therefore emphasized representation, transformation, and assumption diagnostics.

**Classification**

The Crime Classification problem emphasized multiclass prediction.

The results demonstrated that:

  •	  accuracy alone can be misleading;
  •	  class-level performance must be examined;
  •	  feature representation affects classification performance;
  •	  tree-based and linear classification methods can produce different performance profiles;
  •	  probability-based metrics provide information that hard-class predictions do not.

The classification analysis therefore emphasized both aggregate and class-level evaluation.

# Model Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the complete Assignment 8 analysis.

## Store Sales Limitations

The Store Sales analysis aggregated the original store-family observations to a single daily sales series.

This approach was useful for implementing the required ETS and ARIMA models but necessarily discarded information about individual stores and product families.

The resulting models therefore address aggregate daily sales rather than the complete hierarchical structure of the competition.

The validation period also contained only 16 observations. A small validation window means that individual unusual days can have a substantial effect on the calculated error metrics.

The analysis also treated four missing Christmas observations as zero sales after establishing that they corresponded to Christmas holidays. Although this decision is supported by the structure of the data, it remains an explicit modeling assumption.

Finally, the required models did not fully exploit potentially informative exogenous variables such as promotions, store characteristics, holidays, and other economic information.

## House Prices Limitations

The House Prices analysis used a single validation split containing 292 observations.

A different validation split could produce different numerical estimates of model performance.

The engineered linear model also depends on the selected subset of predictors and transformations.

Although the polynomial and interaction terms were required by the assignment, the exact functional form remains an approximation to the underlying relationship between property characteristics and sale price.

The PCA model also demonstrates an important limitation of dimension reduction: retaining 95.07% of predictor variance does not necessarily mean retaining 95.07% of predictive information about the response.

PCA is unsupervised with respect to the response, so components explaining substantial predictor variance are not necessarily the components most useful for predicting SalePrice.

## Crime Classification Limitations

The Crime Classification problem contains many response categories, making accurate prediction inherently difficult.

Class imbalance can cause accuracy to provide an incomplete representation of performance.

The validation sample may also contain temporal and geographic relationships with the training sample. Consequently, the reported validation performance should not automatically be interpreted as an estimate of performance under every possible future deployment scenario.

The classification models also use only the selected feature representation. Important information not represented in those predictors cannot be learned by the algorithms.

Finally, the local validation results and Kaggle leaderboard results evaluate different observations and should not be expected to match.

# Overall Conclusions

Assignment 8 demonstrates the development and evaluation of predictive models across forecasting, regression, and classification problems.

##Store Sales Conclusion

The Store Sales analysis identified substantial temporal structure in aggregate daily sales.
Weekly seasonality was particularly strong, with Sunday and Saturday having the highest average sales and Thursday having the lowest average sales among the reported days.

The analysis also identified substantial New Year's Day effects and confirmed that the missing Christmas observations corresponded to meaningful calendar events.

Both required forecasting models improved substantially upon the naive benchmarks.

  -   ETS produced a validation MAE of 82,459.79 and RMSE of 113,065.78.
  -   ARIMA(1,1,1) produced a validation MAE of 98,728.22 and RMSE of 111,986.09.

The 7-day moving average produced a slightly lower validation RMSE of 109,822.48.

These findings demonstrate that recent local sales information was highly useful for the short forecasting horizon and that model complexity did not automatically produce the lowest error.

The required ETS and ARIMA models nevertheless provided useful and interpretable statistical representations of the series.

## House Prices Conclusion

The House Prices analysis demonstrated the importance of feature engineering, transformation, and dimensionality considerations.

The engineered linear regression incorporated the required polynomial and interaction terms and used a log-transformed response.

It achieved a validation Log RMSE of 0.1704 and Log R² of 0.8244.

The PCA Ridge model reduced the encoded predictor space from 290 variables to 71 components while retaining approximately 95.07% of the predictor variance.

However, its validation Log RMSE of 0.1962 was higher than the engineered linear model's 0.1704.

This finding demonstrates that dimensionality reduction does not necessarily improve predictive accuracy.

The engineered linear model was therefore selected for final model development according to the prespecified validation Log RMSE criterion.

## Crime Classification Conclusion

The San Francisco Crime Classification analysis demonstrated the importance of evaluating multiclass models using multiple metrics.

The Decision Tree achieved:
  
  •	  Accuracy = 0.2683
  •	  Macro F1 = 0.0901
  •	  Weighted F1 = 0.2254
  •	  Log loss = 6.0718

The Random Forest achieved:

  •	  Accuracy = 0.2821
  •	  Macro F1 = 0.0693
  •	  Weighted F1 = 0.2055
  •	  Log loss = 2.4049

The Linear SVM achieved:
  
  •	  Accuracy = 0.2817
  •	  Macro F1 = 0.0885
  •	  Weighted F1 = 0.2318

The models therefore produced different performance profiles.

The Random Forest had the highest reported validation accuracy and substantially lower log loss than the Decision Tree.

The SVM produced nearly identical accuracy to the Random Forest while achieving higher reported macro and weighted F1 values.

The Decision Tree produced the highest reported macro F1.

These results demonstrate why multiclass classification should not be evaluated using accuracy alone.

## Overall Modeling Conclusion

The most important conclusion across Assignment 8 is that predictive modeling requires more than selecting an algorithm and calculating one performance statistic.

The analysis required:

  -   1.	understanding the structure of each dataset;
  -   2.	constructing appropriate features;
  -   3.	separating training and validation observations;
  -   4.	selecting models using out-of-sample evidence;
  -   5.	investigating assumptions;
  -   6.	examining diagnostic artifacts;
  -   7.	comparing multiple evaluation metrics;
  -   8.	generating competition predictions; and
  -   9.	distinguishing local validation from external Kaggle evaluation.

The results also demonstrate that more complicated methods do not automatically produce better predictions.

A simple moving average was competitive with the required Store Sales forecasting models.

The engineered linear regression outperformed the PCA Ridge alternative on validation Log RMSE despite using a substantially different representation.

The Crime Classification models produced similar accuracy but materially different class-level and probability-based metrics.

These findings reinforce the importance of matching the modeling approach and evaluation strategy to the structure of the prediction problem.

Finally, the Kaggle submissions provide an external evaluation of the generated predictions. Local validation results were used for model development and selection, while Kaggle scores provide a separate assessment using hidden competition targets.
